sections.html:
Spanish Fork is a Utah County city at the crossing of Interstate 15 and US-6. Salt Lake City lies about 50 miles north and Provo about 10 miles north, with the Wasatch Range to the east and Utah Lake to the northwest. Springville is about 4 miles northeast, Salem about 4.5 miles south and Payson about 6 miles southwest. The elevation is near 4,666 feet.

Property tax here is a Utah County matter, and the assessor, treasurer and recorder all work from Provo. Nebo School District operates the public schools.

Housing measureSpanish Fork, 2020 to 2024
Population, 2020 count42,602
Population, 2010 count34,691
Owner-occupied housing rate80.4%
Median value of owner-occupied homes$481,500
Median gross rent$1,489
Persons per household3.59

Owners live in most homes, and households run large. Treat the median as a rough survey number, since a given house can price far from it. Permits issued in 2022 covered 810 new homes, 190 single-family and 620 multi-family, so an older property is competing against fresh construction.

I-15 runs north to Salt Lake City and south toward Las Vegas. US-6 climbs east through Spanish Fork Canyon toward Denver. SR-51 and Main Street bring in more traffic, and Union Pacific trains pass through town. Main Street and US-6 carry about 60,000 vehicles per day, and the average commute is 20.0 minutes.

Families will ask about schools. Spanish Fork High and Maple Mountain High are the main high schools, Spanish Fork Junior High and Diamond Fork Middle cover the middle grades, Landmark High is an alternative school and American Leadership Academy is a K to 12 charter. Fifteen of the district's roughly 50 schools are inside the city limits. Ask the district about the school for a specific address before you name one to a buyer.

Commuters also care about road access. A house close to the I-15 and US-6 junction is easy to reach from the rest of the county, which is worth saying in a description.

Winter and water are the two local quirks. The city averages 66 inches of snow and 21.88 inches of rain a year, at a mean temperature of 52.1 degrees Fahrenheit. Roof and furnace condition therefore weigh heavily with buyers.

Two separate systems deliver water. One supplies indoor drinking water, and a pressurized irrigation network feeds lawns and landscaping. With a yard, expect buyers to ask if the irrigation hookup works and what it costs in season.

The city also operates Spanish Fork Power & Light, where the average monthly residential bill is $77.11, and Spanish Fork Community Network for fiber, phone and cable. Natural gas comes from Dominion Energy.

The city permits a single ADU for each single-family home, provided the owner lives on site.

  • The lot must be at least 6,000 square feet, and ADUs are barred in A-E, R-4, R-5 and R-O zones.
  • Parking: three off-street spaces for an internal ADU and four for a detached ADU.
  • Each ADU must register every year with Community Development through CitizenServe for a $60 fee.
  • Impact fees and a separate electric meter are not required.

Registration renews yearly, so show a buyer the current paperwork for any unit you advertise. Reach the Building Division at 801-804-4540.

The county sends the tax notice in the second half of October, and payment is due by November 30. A residence you live in is 45% exempt, which makes 55% of its market value taxable.

Delinquent amounts from earlier years are absent from the current bill, so request a payoff figure from the Treasurer before closing. Visit 100 East Center Street, Suite 1200 in Provo, or call 801-851-8255. Online payment is available. The Recorder, in Suite 1300, answers at 801-851-8179.

Your valuation notice comes first, and it explains how to appeal to the Board of Equalization. File by September 15, or 45 days after the notice was mailed when that is later. For a value you believe is too high, line up comparable sales and repair quotes before you submit.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works in Spanish Fork
sections.html:
Showing proof of funds takes the place of loan approval, which leaves title work as the main clock. You describe the house and when you want to move, look over the offer and sign a purchase agreement.

A title or escrow company handles settlement, the deed goes to the Utah County Recorder and taxes are prorated up to the closing date. Collect roof and furnace dates, any ADU registration, irrigation details and a recent utility bill beforehand. For an inherited house or a job move, closing on your own schedule can be worth more than a slightly higher price.

sections.h2: Selling a house that has an ADU
sections.html:
An ADU can raise value or raise questions. Buyers ask if the unit is registered, if it satisfies the lot and parking rules and if someone rents it now. Keep the registration papers handy, plus the lease and rent history when there is a tenant.

A unit that was never registered leaves two options. Bring it into compliance before listing, or sell as is to a cash buyer who handles the unit later. The right pick depends on the cost of compliance and your preferred closing speed.

Old taxes will not block a sale. The title company lists them as a payoff on the closing statement and deducts them from your proceeds. Phone the Treasurer in Provo for the number, because earlier-year balances are not on this year's bill, and pass it to the title company soon.

This year's tax is divided at the closing date. When November 30 is near, decide who writes the check and record that choice in the purchase agreement.

sections.h2: Steps from first call to closing
sections.html:
1. Send us the address, a description of the house and your target move date.
  2. We look at the house and return a written offer.
  3. On acceptance, you sign a purchase agreement and a title company opens the file.
  4. Title staff verify ownership, taxes and liens.
  5. You sign the closing papers, the deed is recorded in Provo and your proceeds are released.

No lender sits in the middle, so the date you pick and the title work set the pace.

• An ADU that was never registered, or one that violates lot rules.
  • Irrigation or yard problems that a buyer finds on a walkthrough.
  • A roof or furnace aged by years of heavy snow.
  • A tight budget when you have already bought elsewhere.

Deal with any that apply before the first showing, or raise them when you request a cash offer.

faqs.q: Is Spanish Fork in Utah County?
faqs.a: Yes. County offices in Provo handle valuation, tax and deed recording, and public schools are run by Nebo School District.

faqs.q: When are Spanish Fork property taxes due?
faqs.a: Payment is due by November 30, and the county mails the notice in the second half of October.

faqs.q: How many people live in Spanish Fork?
faqs.a: The 2020 count was 42,602, up from 34,691 in 2010.

faqs.q: Can I rent out a basement apartment in Spanish Fork?
faqs.a: Only as a registered ADU. The owner has to live on site, the lot needs at least 6,000 square feet and registration costs $60 a year. Confirm the details on the city's ADU page.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Spanish Fork?
faqs.a: The survey median is $481,500 for owner-occupied homes in 2020 to 2024. Your own house could price well above or below that figure.
